answer: LINE addresses sparse neighborhoods in low-degree vertices by not relying solely on second-order proximity for every node. In the second-order model, each vertex is represented by a source embedding and a context embedding, and the model learns to predict a node’s neighborhood distribution from observed edges. For low-degree vertices, the neighborhood context is inherently sparse, so the second-order objective can be noisy or weakly constrained. LINE mitigates this by combining first-order proximity and second-order proximity objectives in the full model, so even when a vertex has too few neighbors to support reliable second-order inference, its embedding can still be informed by direct edge-preserving first-order signals. In practice, LINE also uses negative sampling and stochastic optimization to make learning feasible on large sparse graphs, but it does not introduce a special separate inference rule specifically for low-degree vertices; instead, the shared embedding objectives and observed graph structure provide the training signal. Thus, low-degree vertices are handled implicitly through the joint optimization framework rather than by an explicit sparse-neighborhood correction mechanism.
